title: The Semester of Westbrook High
premise: In Westbrook, population 903, Jonah Voss has perfected invisibility — until an anonymous group chat called 'The Forecast' starts posting predictions that come true with eerie precision, and one of them names him. As the predictions escalate from pranks to a deadly bus-crash warning, Jonah realizes the chat's author is someone at Westbrook High using him as a pawn, and the only way to stop the final prophecy is to expose truths the whole town has buried — including what really happened the night his best friend Eli's older brother died. To survive the season's last game, Jonah must come out twice over: as the kid he is, and as the witness everyone paid him to stay silent. The chat is shut down, but the town's reckoning has only begun.
about_author: Tamsin Fairweather is the pen name of a former small-town substitute teacher who spent three years collecting the unspoken stories of rural high schools. They write young adult fiction about kids who learn that surviving quietly is not the same as living.

chapters.title: Head Down, Grades Up
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Establishes Westbrook High's social map and Jonah's survival rules: don't draw eyes, don't correct anyone, don't let the locker door hang open too long. Emotional beat: the exhausting arithmetic of invisibility, and the small warmth of his one friendship with Eli.

chapters.title: Nine Hundred Strangers
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, morning bus ride. We see the town's intimacy — everyone's business is everyone's — and the memorial plaque for Caleb Marsh, Eli's older brother, dead four years. Beat: grief as the town's shared weather.

chapters.title: The First Message
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. An unknown number adds him to a group chat called The Forecast: 'Tomorrow, third period, the fire alarm goes off. Don't be in the hallway.' Beat: curiosity warring with his rule about attention.

chapters.title: Third Period
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The alarm rings at exactly the predicted minute. He watches classmates laugh it off as a prank; he alone knows he was warned. Beat: the first crack in his invisibility — someone sees him.

chapters.title: Rules of the Forecast
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. More predictions land: a pop quiz, a cancelled game, a teacher's resignation. The chat's tone shifts from playful to commanding. Beat: Jonah tests the predictions and finds them flawless, and frightening.

chapters.title: Eli Doesn't Believe in Ghosts
chapters.summary: Eli's POV. Eli notices Jonah checking his phone like it's a wound. Their friendship is built on not asking questions — Caleb's death is the question neither asks. Beat: loyalty as mutual silence.

chapters.title: Named
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The Forecast posts: 'Jonah Voss knows. Ask him what happened at the quarry.' The chat turns its thousand-watt attention on him. Beat: terror of exposure — the thing he's spent years avoiding.

chapters.title: The Quarry Question
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, flashback woven in. Four years ago, twelve-year-old Jonah saw something at the quarry the night Caleb died, and an adult told him what to say. Beat: the buried cost of survival — his silence was purchased.

chapters.title: Hallway Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Classmates circle: Priya the editor, Deke the quarterback, Mara who runs the anonymous confession account. Everyone wants to know what Jonah knows. Beat: being seen is worse than being invisible.

chapters.title: Priya's Theory
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. The school-paper editor treats The Forecast as a story, not a haunting. She maps the predictions and finds one gap: the chat never predicts anything about itself. Beat: intellectual thrill, first ally.

chapters.title: Deke's Debt
chapters.summary: Deke's POV. The quarterback got a prediction that saved him from a failed drug test — and now the chat owns him. Beat: the price of survival, and how quickly a favor becomes a leash.

chapters.title: Homecoming, Interrupted
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The Forecast predicts the homecoming bonfire will 'end early.' It does — a propane tank, a small explosion, no one hurt but no one laughing either. Beat: the game has turned real.

chapters.title: What Jonah Almost Said
chapters.summary: Eli's POV. Eli confronts Jonah: you know something about The Forecast, maybe about Caleb. Jonah lies. Beat: the friendship's first real fracture, felt like a bone breaking.

chapters.title: The Sheriff's Son
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara reveals she's been scraping the chat's metadata — it routes through the school's own servers. The list of suspects is short. Beat: the hunt becomes internal; the predator is a classmate.

chapters.title: Locker 114
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. A note in his locker, handwritten: 'You were there. Say it before the last game or the Forecast says it for you.' Beat: deadline established — the season finale is the fuse.

chapters.title: Coach Marsh
chapters.summary: Coach's POV. Eli's father, coaching his last season, watches Jonah with an expression Jonah can't read — gratitude or warning. Beat: the adult who bought Jonah's silence, now aging into his lie.

chapters.title: The List of Liars
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Priya and Jonah cross-reference: who benefits from Caleb's death being an accident? The sheriff, the coach, the quarry owner — half the town's power structure. Beat: justice outside the law starts to look like the only kind available.

chapters.title: Snow Day
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. School cancels; Jonah and Priya dig through the library's old yearbooks and a microfilm of the accident report. Beat: quiet intimacy between two kids building a case out of paper.

chapters.title: The Report Doesn't Add Up
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The official story: Caleb fell. But the quarry's lower ledge was fenced that autumn — a fence that appears in no photo from that night. Beat: the lie has a shape now, and it's load-bearing.

chapters.title: Deke Breaks
chapters.summary: Deke's POV. The Forecast orders Deke to sabotage the team's playoff chances; he refuses and is threatened with exposure. Beat: the leash tightens; Deke becomes a mirror of what Jonah could become.

chapters.title: Mara's Mistake
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara gets too close to identifying the chat's author and is doxxed — her family's secrets dumped into the group chat. Beat: the cost of investigating; fear spreads through the school like flu.

chapters.title: Jonah's Mother
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. His mom, who moved them to Westbrook to disappear from their old life, senses Jonah is drowning. He almost tells her everything — and tells her half. Beat: the loneliness of partial truth.

chapters.title: The Second-to-Last Game
chapters.summary: Eli's POV. Eli plays angry, takes a dirty hit, and in the aftermath finally says Caleb's name out loud to Jonah for the first time in four years. Beat: grief spoken aloud; the wall between them cracking.

chapters.title: What I Saw
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah tells Eli the truth: he saw Coach Marsh and the quarry owner arguing with Caleb that night, and was told by the sheriff — Deke's father — that a boy who talked would ruin two families. Beat: confession; the friendship tested at its breaking point.

chapters.title: The Silence Between Us
chapters.summary: Eli's POV. Eli walks away — not from the truth, but from the four years Jonah let him grieve a lie. Beat: the blurb's promised cost; the friendship pays it.

chapters.title: The Forecast Names Its Price
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Final prediction posted: 'At the last game, the bleachers on the home side fail. Unless Jonah Voss tells the town what he saw.' Beat: the chat weaponizes his silence against the whole town.

chapters.title: Evacuate a Believer
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. No adult will act on a prophecy from a group chat. Jonah and Priya must manufacture evidence — a structural inspection request, an anonymous tip — to empty the bleachers. Beat: justice outside the law, engineered by teenagers.

chapters.title: Deke's Choice
chapters.summary: Deke's POV. The chat orders Deke to keep the bleachers full by promising fans a record night. Instead, Deke posts everything the chat ever made him do. Beat: the leash breaks from the inside.

chapters.title: The Last Game of the Season
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Friday night lights, packed bleachers, Jonah standing at the fence with a bullhorn he doesn't know how to use. Beat: the whole book converging on one breath before speech.

chapters.title: Jonah Voss Speaks
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Over the PA, borrowed from the announcer's booth, Jonah tells nine hundred people what he saw at the quarry — and, in the same breath, that he's the only out kid in town saying it. Beat: double coming-out; terror transfigured into voice.

chapters.title: The Bleachers Hold
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs, braided. Half the crowd leaves on Jonah's warning; the section that stays groans but holds — the prediction was a bluff, or a test. Beat: relief and fury in equal measure; the town turns on the chat.

chapters.title: Unmasking
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. With Deke's dump and Priya's metadata, they trace The Forecast to the last person anyone suspected: the sheriff's department intern, Caleb's cousin, who'd spent four years trying to force the town's truth out the only way a kid could. Beat: the antagonist reframed as a wounded mirror of Jonah.

chapters.title: What the Chat Wanted
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, conversation with the intern. She never meant harm to Jonah; she needed a witness and blackmailed the only one who had one. Beat: grief recognizing grief; no clean villain.

chapters.title: The Sheriff's Office
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah gives a formal statement, on the record, with his mother beside him. The sheriff who silenced him resigns by morning. Beat: justice through the system, barely — and only because kids forced it.

chapters.title: Coach Marsh's Press Conference
chapters.summary: Eli's POV. Eli's father admits his cover-up — not the death itself, but the silence after. Eli watches his father choose truth too late to save his job, but not too late to save something else. Beat: accountability as inheritance.

chapters.title: Empty Locker, Open Door
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah returns to school as the kid who talked. Some doors close — old friends, safe silences — but the hallway looks different when you're not hiding in it. Beat: the price paid, itemized, and survivable.

chapters.title: Eli at the Fence
chapters.summary: Eli's POV. Eli finds Jonah at the quarry fence, where the story started. 'You should have told me in ninth grade,' he says. 'But you told me.' Beat: forgiveness without erasure — the friendship reformed, scarred but real.

chapters.title: The Last Edition
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. The school paper runs the full investigation under real bylines. Mara's confession account becomes a verified tip line. Beat: the tools of the chat turned into instruments of accountability.

chapters.title: Spring, Population 903
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The town is smaller and more honest than it was. Jonah registers for a summer journalism program; his mom finally asks about the old life, and he answers. Beat: identity no longer a hiding place but an address.

chapters.title: The Semester of Westbrook High
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, closing. At the final bell, Jonah leaves his locker door open — a small, deliberate act no one else notices. The Forecast chat is deleted; its last message, sent by Jonah, reads simply: 'It already happened.' Beat: the prophecy fulfilled by being spoken; survival transformed into living.
